elements.char: Abstract
elements.label: text

elements.char: This paper provides a general equilibrium approach to pricing volatility. Existing models
elements.label: text

elements.char: (e.g., ARCH/GARCH, stochastic volatility) take a statistical approach to estimating volatility,
elements.label: text

elements.char: volatility indices (e.g., CBOE VIX) use a weighted combination of options, and utility based
elements.label: text

elements.char: models assume a specific type of preferences. In contrast we treat volatility as an asset and
elements.label: text

elements.char: price it using the general equilibrium state pricing framework. Our results show that the gen-
elements.label: text

elements.char: eral equilibrium volatility method developed in this paper provides superior forecasting ability
elements.label: text

elements.char: for realized volatility and serves as an effective fear gauge. We demonstrate the flexibility
elements.label: text

elements.char: and generality of our approach by pricing downside risk and upside opportunity. Finally, we
elements.label: text

elements.char: show that the superior forecasting ability of our approach generates significant economic
elements.label: text

elements.char: value through volatility timing.
elements.label: text

elements.char: Introduction
elements.label: text

elements.char: Volatility modelling has proceeded as a field separate from asset pricing. Statistical models,
elements.label: text

elements.char: such as ARCH [1, 2], GARCH [3], stochastic volatility [4], and option prices [5] are commonly
elements.label: text

elements.char: used to estimate volatility, without reference to modern asset pricing theory. In this paper, we
elements.label: text

elements.char: propose to
elements.label: text

elements.char: price
elements.label: text

elements.char: volatility using a general equilibrium asset-pricing framework. The advantage
elements.label: text

elements.char: of such an approach is that volatility can be priced and measured in the most general setting
elements.label: text

elements.char: available. The approach also allows us to extend measurement and pricing (such as downside
elements.label: text

elements.char: risk pricing and upside opportunity pricing), which cannot be achieved with current
elements.label: text

elements.char: approaches to volatility modelling.
elements.label: text
